name: Kojic acid soap

lead: Kojic acid is a compound made by several fungi, including Aspergillus oryzae, and is a by-product of sake brewing. In skincare it is used to lighten skin and treat uneven pigmentation such as melasma; soap is one of the formats it comes in.
In looksmaxxing forums, people mention it alongside glutathione and lycopene when aiming for a particular skin tone or undertone, for example evening out or changing colour balance.

paras: It is a wash-off cleanser used in a normal washing routine, usually alongside sunscreen and other brightening ingredients. Users report buying it from mainstream online retailers.

Animal studies suggest weak carcinogenicity, though it is not believed to reach carcinogenic thresholds on human skin at cosmetic levels. The EU now limits it to 1% in face and hand products from 1 November 2025. Lightening soaps can cause irritation in some users.

angle.text: People use kojic acid cleansers to even out skin tone or lighten pigmentation. Wash-off soaps contact skin briefly, and users often pair them with other brightening products.

lead: Kojic acid soap is a bar or liquid cleanser containing kojic acid, a skin-lightening ingredient made by fungi such as Aspergillus oryzae and a by-product of sake brewing. Cosmetics use it to lighten skin and treat melasma.[1]

In looksmaxxing forums, users discuss it as part of a skin-tone stack with other ingredients such as glutathione and lycopene, aiming for a preferred undertone or an even complexion. One looksmax.org poster describes wanting a "red undertone" tan look and says they bought the soap on Amazon.[2]

Regulators have addressed the ingredient: the EU added it to Annex III of its Cosmetics Regulation, allowing face and hand products at up to 1% for products placed on the market from 1 November 2025.[1]
infobox: 1% in face and hand products (from Nov 2025)

paras: Kojic acid is an organic chelating agent that forms a red complex with ferric iron. It is described as a mild inhibitor of pigment formation and is also used to stop cut fruit browning and as a precursor to the flavour compound maltol.[1]

Some animal studies suggest weak carcinogenicity, but the compound is not believed to reach carcinogenic thresholds in human skin and is regarded as safe at cosmetic-use levels; its hazard classification includes H351, suspected of causing cancer.[1] In the EU, Regulation 2024/996 allows it only in face and hand products at up to 1%, for products marketed from 1 November 2025.[1]
A looksmax.org thread about receiving glutathione, lycopene and kojic acid soap shows the product framed as a way to shift undertone toward red, with the poster noting summer tanning as a factor.[2]
No studies found on kojic acid soap specifically.

lore.intro: Kojic acid soap appears in forum discussions of skin-tone and undertone changes, usually alongside oral supplements.[2]

claims.claim: Kojic acid soap plus glutathione and lycopene can give a red-undertone tan.
